content: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is an antiretroviral medication used in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. It is typically administered orally at a dose of 300 mg once daily. TDF is also available in combination formulations, such as Truvada (with emtricitabine), Atripla (with emtricitabine and efavirenz), and Complera (with emtricitabine and rilpivirine). Additionally, TDF is indicated for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B at the same dosage of 300 mg orally once daily. For patients with renal impairment, dosage adjustments are necessary based on creatinine clearance (CrCl) levels: CrCl ≥ 50 mL/min: No dosage adjustment is required. CrCl 30–49 mL/min: Administer 300 mg orally every 48 hours. CrCl 10–29 mL/min: Administer 300 mg orally every 72–96 hours. CrCl < 10 mL/min: Not studied. Hemodialysis: Administer 300 mg orally every 7 days or after approximately 12 hours of dialysis. TDF has an orphan drug designation for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus. Before initiating treatment, patients should be tested for both HBV and HIV-1 infections. Baseline assessments should include serum creatinine, estimated CrCl, urine glucose, and urine protein. In patients with chronic kidney disease, serum phosphorus levels should also be evaluated. In pediatric patients aged 2 years and older, TDF is indicated for the treatment of HIV infection and chronic hepatitis B. The recommended dose is 8 mg/kg orally once daily, not exceeding 300 mg per day. Safety and efficacy in children under 2 years of age have not been established. No specific dosage recommendations are available for pediatric patients with renal impairment. TDF should not be co-administered with certain drugs due to potential interactions that may increase toxicity or reduce efficacy. For example: Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir (a complete HIV regimen): Should not be combined with other antiretrovirals. Streptozocin: Increases nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity; contraindicated. Adefovir: Enhances nephrotoxicity; avoid co-administration. Bacitracin: Increases nephrotoxicity; avoid concurrent use. Cyclosporine: Increases nephrotoxicity; use caution. NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac): May increase TDF levels and toxicity due to reduced renal clearance; monitor closely or consider alternatives. Amphotericin B formulations: Increase nephrotoxicity and TDF levels; use caution. Cisplatin and other nephrotoxic agents: Increase nephrotoxicity and TDF levels; monitor closely. Drugs affecting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) or BCRP transporters (e.g., ledipasvir, elagolix, encorafenib): May increase TDF levels or toxicity; monitor and adjust doses as needed. TDF may also interact with other medications by altering renal clearance or competing for active tubular secretion, leading to increased serum concentrations of TDF or the co-administered drug. Examples include: Didanosine: Increased risk of pancreatitis; reduce didanosine dose. Metformin: Increased risk of lactic acidosis; monitor closely. Digoxin: Increased toxicity risk; monitor levels. Entecavir: Increased toxicity risk; monitor closely. Certain combinations may increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome, such as with efavirenz, emtricitabine, or atazanavir. In these cases, close monitoring is recommended.
